title: Augmenting Imaginary-Time Evolution with Local Geometric Information
authors: Carlos L. Benavides-Riveros, Prachi Sharma, Fedor Šimkovic
abstract: Imaginary-time evolution (ITE) underpins a broad family of algorithms for ground-state preparation in quantum simulation and quantum many-body physics. In these methods, convergence is governed by the energy variance of the instantaneous state, causing the flow to approach the ground state only asymptotically. We introduce an augmented imaginary-time evolution (AITE) framework that replaces the standard gradient flow on the energy landscape with a geometrically informed descent along locally optimal directions, which are identified by exploiting the higher-order statistical structure of the instantaneous energy distribution. The resulting flow strictly outperforms standard ITE throughout the entire evolution and exhibits two qualitatively distinct regimes: a superlinear convergence regime, followed by an extinction regime in which the energy error vanishes exactly at a finite imaginary time, in sharp contrast to the asymptotic exponential decay of ITE. Standard ITE is recovered in the zero-skewness limit of AITE, implying that the acceleration extends naturally across the broader ITE algorithmic family.
summary: The paper introduces Augmented Imaginary-Time Evolution (AITE) to accelerate the notoriously slow convergence of standard imaginary-time evolution algorithms. By incorporating local geometric information derived from energy distribution statistics, AITE achieves superlinear convergence leading to finite-time error extinction. This provides a significant algorithmic improvement for simulating ground states in quantum many-body systems.
main_problem: Standard imaginary-time evolution (ITE) for ground-state preparation converges only asymptotically, leading to slow convergence rates.
main_result: The proposed Augmented Imaginary-Time Evolution (AITE) framework achieves superlinear convergence and exhibits finite-time extinction of the energy error, significantly outperforming standard ITE.
method: AITE augments the standard gradient flow by incorporating local geometric information derived from higher-order statistical moments (like skewness) of the instantaneous energy distribution into the descent direction.
model_or_system: The methods are applied to general quantum many-body systems, with specific numerical tests performed on the H8 chain and the Fermi-Hubbard model. The evolution is governed by imaginary time ($	au$) under a Hamiltonian $\hat{H}$.
key_observables: Energy error $E(	au) - E_{	ext{GS}}$, energy variance ($\mu_2$), and skewness coefficient ($\kappa$).
important_parameters: The spectral gap ($\Delta = E_1 - E_{GS}$), the imaginary time $	au$, and the target precision $\epsilon^*$.
main_assumptions: Practical implementation restricts the search for optimal descent operators to the second-order Krylov subspace, and mean-field approximations are used for higher moments.
figures_summary: Figures compare energy error vs. time ($	au$) curves, showing AITE's power-law extinction against ITE's asymptotic exponential decay across various models (H8 chain, Fermi-Hubbard).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem with standard ITE, develops the AITE framework by generalizing the flow using geometric information ($\hat{O}(	au)$), analyzes the convergence rate improvement leading to finite-time extinction, and discusses practical approximations like mean-field moment estimation.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful algorithmic acceleration technique for finding ground states in strongly correlated systems, directly impacting computational methods used in condensed matter physics simulations.

The main panel shows the error evolution on a logarithmic scale, with shaded regions identi- fying four dynamical regimes: the linear regime (ε ≫∆/4, blue), the superlinear regime (ε ∼∆/4, green), the power-law extinction regime (ε ≪∆/4, red), and the asymptotic ITE regime. The dashed vertical line marks the finite extinction time τ ∗of AITE. The inset displays the same dynamics on a linear scale, highlighting the finite-time extinction of AITE in contrast to the asymptotic exponential decay of ITE.
